Level $n$ is therefore most sensitive to $\delta V$ near its own turning points. It is completely insensitive to $\delta V$ beyond them, apart from the exponentially small tails. But the weight is not concentrated there. The level responds to $\delta V$ everywhere inside $[a,b]$; in the linear well, for example, the outer tenth of the distance carries only about a third of the weight (Sample Problem below). What changes sharply at the turning point is the response to $\delta V$ \emph{beyond} it: outside $[a,b]$ the wavefunction decays exponentially, so level $n$ barely feels $\delta V$ there. In an even, monotone well each level index $n$ is thus attached to a position $x_{E_n}$, the outer edge of the region it probes. But in \cref{eq:wkb-smooth} the count comes from a potential through $\Phi(E)/\pi$, whereas $\Nfl$ is a sum over primes (Eq.~(4)); no potential, Hamiltonian or wavefunction appears.
